title: A uniform Hilbert transform estimate for Lipschitz directions
main_claim: Take any planar unit vector field v with Lip(v) ≤ 1. The truncated directional Hilbert transform with |t| between ε and a fixed absolute a_* is bounded on L^2 with an absolute constant, uniformly in the inner truncation ε. Hence the principal value is strongly L^2 bounded, which settles Stein's weak-(2,2) conjecture at outer length a_*/Lip(v).

The ordinary estimate (eq:src-4) and the reverse-disparity estimate depend on them, and eq:src-10 reuses the synthesis lemma. Their conclusions match known Lacey–Li-type estimates: restricted weak (2,2) on one band for measurable slopes, and an L^p-type gain for |E|<|F|. This is a coverage limitation, not an identified gap.

issues.description: This does not break the proof. The whole improvement rests on the exponent decrease δ_L ≈ c_ph/(C_D √L log L), with c_ph = 2^{-60}. It beats the L^C losses only for astronomically large L, and all the asymptotic orderings (B^{100} ≪ m, m^C τ → 0, pK_* = G^{o(1)}) also assume L is that large. The logic is sound because every threshold is absolute, but the theorem is purely qualitative and C_* is not effective in any practical sense.

- Sec. 2 reductions: localization and rotation; endpoint replacement; the amplitude-summation lemma; the Carleson embedding and Lipschitz commutator (I checked the conjugation-derivative identity); random-sign band reassembly; time reduction; scale truncation; narrow bins with the m^4 τ commutator error; bin amplitude levels; packet representation (normalized symbol coordinates); and Prop. red:model-suffices.
- Sec. 4 popular forest: the Lacey–Li Kakeya application, including the admissibility of the arc and the length clipping; the weak-L^2 top count; the mask lemma.
- Sec. 5: line moments (John–Nirenberg, annular 3-variation via Lépingle/JSW), top-good corollary, mask removal and eq:src-12.
- Sec. 6 simultaneous separated count: the line lemma's Carleson and exponential-moment argument, and the Lipschitz witness transfer, whose inequalities I verified.
- Sec. 7 finite Fourier gain, in full. Checked: unique completion; the Hölder and Cauchy–Schwarz Hellinger bounds; TV ≤ sqrt(1−H^2); the quantile triple-event deficit giving δ_κ = κ^4(1−κ/2)^2/4096; δ_{κ0} = 2^{-54} > c_ph; the dominant-coefficient expansion 1+14b^2 ≤ (1+b^{r4})^{4/r4}; constant-one Riesz–Thorin giving 1/r_* = 1−(α−1)/p; the Hilbert-valued Minkowski steps.
- Sec. 8 hierarchy: eligible masses; m_v and the retention probability π_c ≥ n_c/m_c; the cancellation π_c^{1−r}|λ_c|^r ≤ 1; full-root variation; amplitude bounds; mass and amplitude motion at scales H_j (checked H_j/l_* = 1/(B^2√G) and the phase ρ_{j+1}H_j/w = G^{-1/2}); good paths; the exact path expansion and its probability argument; marking.
- Sec. 9 prediction: separation Q/w versus ν_I bandwidth G^{5/8}ρ_{j+1}/(4w); averaging ∫β̃ dν ≤ 1; comparison and blending; the change to uniform measure with a loss proportional to υ; step suprema.
- Sec. 10 residuals: marked square summation; the unary energy telescope and its V* subsolution; the 3-variation Hölder step; the choice of M; mesh-averaging of ∏Γ_j.
- Sec. 11: vertex estimate, simplex three-lines with Gaussian damping, central exponent 1+(2−α)/p+μ/K, boundary averaging telescope, exceptional-set budgets (e^{-5L/2}), final assembly.

Not audited in detail: Sec. 3 size lemma and separated-synthesis lemma (lines ~147–440), and parts of the tree-bound proof.
